learningObjectives.title: Technology (Google effect, social media, digital health)

options: A cultural dimension used to compare cultures
questions.explain: It contrasts emphasis on the individual with emphasis on the group.

questions.q: Applying a culturally specific questionnaire unchanged to another culture risks:
questions.explain: Treating one culture's tool as universal is an imposed etic and can misrepresent behaviour.

options: From within a specific culture on its own terms
questions.explain: Emic research understands behaviour within a culture; etic compares across cultures.

questions.q: A clinician adapts diagnosis to local expressions of distress and involves community members. This reduces:
questions.explain: Emic sensitivity and local collaboration reduce culture bias in diagnosis.

questions.q: Cultural dimensions such as Hofstede's are criticised for:
options: Generalising whole nations and masking within-culture variation
questions.explain: National averages risk stereotyping and overlook diversity within a culture.

questions.q: Doing an activity because it is interesting in itself is:
questions.explain: Intrinsic motivation comes from within the activity; extrinsic from external rewards.

questions.q: Self-determination theory stresses which needs as drivers of motivation?
questions.explain: SDT identifies autonomy, competence and relatedness as core to intrinsic motivation.

questions.q: The 'overjustification effect' suggests that heavy external rewards can:
questions.explain: Excessive extrinsic rewards can reduce intrinsic interest in a previously enjoyable activity.

questions.q: A health app uses points and streaks to keep users engaged. This relies mainly on:
questions.explain: External incentives such as points are extrinsic motivators; long-term change also needs intrinsic engagement.

questions.q: Readiness to change a health behaviour is described by the:
questions.explain: The transtheoretical model describes precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance.

questions.q: The 'Google effect' (Sparrow et al.) is the tendency to:
options: Remember where to find information rather than the information itself
questions.explain: People offload storage to accessible devices (transactive memory).

questions.q: Evidence on social media and behaviour is best described as:
questions.explain: Most studies are correlational and technology changes fast, so causal claims need caution.

questions.q: A benefit of digital health tools (apps, telehealth) is that they:
questions.explain: They can increase access, though engagement and evidence quality remain concerns.

questions.q: A study links heavy media multitasking with poorer attention filtering. A valid caution is that:
options: Correlation does not establish that multitasking causes the deficit
It proves multitasking harms the brain
questions.explain: Pre-existing differences could explain both, so causation is not established.

questions.q: The HL extension asks students mainly to:
options: Evaluate how culture, motivation and technology shape behaviour within the contexts
questions.explain: The extension deepens the four contexts rather than adding a separate topic.

questions.q: A general methodological caution for technology-and-behaviour research is that it is:
questions.explain: Fast-moving, correlational evidence limits firm causal conclusions.

questions.q: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation differ in that intrinsic motivation is driven by:
options: Interest and satisfaction in the activity itself
questions.explain: Intrinsic motivation is internal to the activity; extrinsic depends on external consequences.

questions.q: Cross-cultural differences in conformity (e.g. higher in collectivist cultures) illustrate that:
questions.explain: Cultural dimensions such as collectivism predict differences in behaviours like conformity.
